segments.text: So, the Rippaverse. They recently signed
a global distribution deal with
Hatchette Book Group, with some treating
it as an I told you so victory lap. I
don't typically give these alternative
facts-based efforts much oxygen, but I
do find the economics interesting. And
it's always good to know where the E.
coli forward taco stand in your
neighborhood sets up. Launched in 2022,
this controversial and purposely vapid
universe filled with pop-tart deep
characters built its footprint through
multi-million dollar direct-to-consumer
crowdfunded campaign. It's not a victory
lap, it's a stress test. Up until now,
this publisher has worked on a
direct-to-consumer allegedly profitable
business model, returnability. In
traditional book publishing, and unlike
the comic book world, retailers are
purchasing those books on a returnable
basis. If a retailer buys that book and
it doesn't sell, they ship it back to
Hatchette to recoup some measure of the
cost. That means the real story is told
six months from now and measured by the
return rate of these books. Once you
look at that data, you can tell whether
there's a genuine widespread interest in
this universe, or if it remains a highly
dedicated, localized niche of dudes
yelling from their front porch.
>> Hey brother, saw your video and first I
want to thank you. Unlike other people
who framed our partnership as a
direct market deal, as if it were just
about comic shops re-releasing floppies,
you correctly classified it as trade,
and you actually walked your audience
through the difference between the two
markets. Most folks don't know graphic
novel format trade from single issue
direct market. So, I appreciate you
getting that right. I am largely
unfamiliar with your content, but I was
tagged in this. But I can tell that
you've got viewers who value what you
do, and I wish you nothing but the best.
You found your niche, and that's a real
thing. I also noticed the Supergirl
poster behind you, so I know I'm talking
to somebody who genuinely loves the
medium. That matters to me far more than
whether we agree or not. And you've made
it clear through some pretty witty words
that you're not a fan of our work,
that's completely your right. You're a
fan of some of the other publishers and
their characters, so the fact that you'd
even turn your attention to a smaller
publisher means something and I do
appreciate it. Now, let me offer some
clarification and perspective because I
think a lot of people can use the
information.
Foundationally, the Rippaverse never
crowdfunded. We ran pre-order campaigns
with public numbers. The books were
already complete whether they shipped
was never contingent on hitting a goal.
It wasn't until 2025 that we launched
our actual crowdfunding brand Rippa
Works, which has run only two campaigns
to date. You did know that we ran
pre-orders, so this may be more of a
semantics thing, but that distinction
does matter. On the Hachette deal and
the returns question that you brought
up, you are right about how the return
process works and I want to give the
audience the fuller picture. First,
trade is an additional channel on top of
our direct-to-consumer business. It's
not a replacement, so a return in a
bookstore doesn't bite into pre-order
revenue. That's already been collected
on the DTC side. Second, returns are
universal, not diagnostic. Every trade
publisher in existence runs meaningful
return rates, including the best
sellers. It's a big in cost of being in
the channel, it's not really a verdict.
Third, this is order-driven, not
speculative stocking. Our books are
available to the trade market and those
customers are requesting them after a
long, information-rich
pre-order process, not stores gambling
shelf space on a name they've never
heard of. Speculative stocking is what
really drives those heavy returns.
Demand pool ordering structurally lowers
that very number you're pointing to.
But, here's the real why. A lot of our
customers, especially international
ones, who struggled with the cost and
the hassle of the shipping, they can now
get our books through traditional
channels. Our D2C performance is
precisely why so many distributors came
to us. The interest was earned. This
deal is about making our books easier to
access, not proving whether the demand
exist. In that sense, the stress test
already happened. And on the 6-month
timeline, because our books were never
in the trade channel to begin with, the
next 6 months wouldn't actually tell you
much anyway. That's not how selling
calendars work. Realistically, you're
looking at well over a year before
there's anything meaningful to measure.
But, the more important thing is keeping
the goal in perspective. It's about
making our books easier to access by
placing them in a channel they simply
weren't in before. We're not trying to
shift our existing base over to the
trade market to prove how widespread it
is. You also framed it as widespread
interest versus a niche, as if it's one
or the other. I push back slightly on
that dichotomy. A dedicated core and an
expanding reach are the normal state of
any growing business. Those aren't
opposites. And niche isn't really a
dirty word. I think we're in an era
where broad mass appeal is increasingly
reserved for legacy IP, legacy studios
and publishers, and the offshoots of
those legacy places. Because they were
built in a different time, and they're
sort of already woven into the culture
with a lot of capital. Which is why
you're going to see more and more niches
that are wildly successful on their own
terms. There's nothing wrong with that.
It's less likely to happen for us at a
legacy scale precisely because we're
new. Plus, we're privately held and we
don't sell off our assets. Remember,
Hachette handles our retail and
wholesale sales and distribution. We're
still the owner and publisher. Now, on
the victory lap bit, I'm not sure
whether you meant us or our fans, but
either way, consider where this started.
We were the underdog. I was a musician,
not a comic book creator. I crossed over
from being a fan to being an independent
publisher from offering opinions,
positive and negative, to actually
putting my money where my mouth was.
That transition was not easy and I've
grown a lot as a professional through
it. A few years ago, I might have
answered a video like this very
differently, but owning a business
that's been this much of a blessing and
becoming a father changes a man. The
Rippaverse mission was always simple.
Build a fun universe and build a fun
environment
>> [music]
>> for both fans and creators. That draws a
base from many different walks of life
and many different social and political
views. A lot people believed in that
vision, which is why when we launched,
it was a million dollars in 30 hours
with Ice on number one. And that was
before any mainstream outlet
decided to cover it. Now, fast forward
to today, we've sold somewhere north of
300,000 books and well over 15 million
dollars in total revenue. And yes, I had
a sizable following before launching,
but that's never the primary determinant
of support. There are people with
smaller followings who have launched
bigger projects than I have, and people
with bigger followings who have done
less than we have. We did this with no
external investors, and we built a real
warehousing operation that's delivered
at a high volume, and that execution is
very important. You're not the first
skeptic, though, and oddly enough, the
skeptics made it easier for people to
root for us. Every milestone lands like
an achievement. We went from the
Ripperverse will never launch to the
Ripperverse will be over in a couple of
years to well, let's see what happens
now that they've reached a market
they've never had access to, a market
that we succeeded without, and we did
all of it with no meaningful positive or
neutral coverage from the mainstream
comic book industry outlets. From an
ambitious idea, we've gotten action
figures from McFarlane Toys, statues
from Iron Studios, animation, and much
more. We're blessed and thankful for it.
And it's important to understand that
this was never a one-man band. It was a
collective effort, a mix of new and
veteran talent, many of whom worked on
characters that you probably enjoyed
from the mainstream. We'll soon have
released over 100 books built by more
than 100 different creators, and I think
that latter point is so important. I
don't think people talk about it enough.
This is not just me. It's not even the I
S.O.M. Verse. So, to close, I know
you're not a fan of our work. If you
gave it a shot, and it wasn't for you,
that's completely understandable, and
nobody should come after you just
because you don't like something. You're
not under any obligation to like
something. I appreciate you giving us a
look. We're far from the only game in
town, and we're not in anybody's way. I
do not see the market as a fixed pie.
Our success doesn't mean we're taking
away from anyone else. Where all
respectfully disagree is your
description of our fans. This isn't our
culture. People defending the things
that they love is part of the deal. I'm
sure you push back on takes about the
work that you enjoy, too. I don't read
that as defensive. Everybody has a right
to their opinion and no single opinion
is the opinion. But, I do want to name
something bigger because I think it's
the real rot underneath most of these
these conversations.
We've reached a point
>> [music]
>> where people don't dislike a thing on
its merits anymore. They dislike it
because of who likes it.
If the wrong crowd or the wrong group or
the wrong person enjoys something,
that's suddenly reason enough to write
it off sight unseen.
The work itself becomes almost
irrelevant [music] and that happens on
all sides. Nobody has clean hands on
this and I'm not even even pretending to
be above it.
That's a shame because this is an
industry and a hobby that's built on
passion. I love for us to get back to
arguing about whether one character can
beat another or whether something was
lore accurate instead of the dissections
we do today where a book
or piece of entertainment gets dismissed
for reasons that have nothing to do with
what's in it. I love for us to get back
to fun. So, to you and to anyone else
who's skeptical of the Ripperverse, I
still value your input. You are free to
your criticism and your analysis and I
genuinely love for you to pull up to our
Discord and meet the team and the fans
and the creators or come see us at a con
and find out what we're actually about.
I'd also extend that offer to speak
privately off the record, obviously, as
social media can be a bit of a spectacle
and it muddies the waters. There are a
lot of preconceived notions in play and
you might walk away with a different
conclusion. And if you don't,
that's fine, [music] too. And to
everybody watching, we hope you'll
consider picking up a book wherever you
get your books.
